title: CAP, PACELC and consistency models
scopeHtml: Scope: CAP, PACELC, consistency models, quorums, conflict resolution, per-feature choices. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Why distributed systems must choose
notes.html:
When data lives on several machines connected by a network, the network can fail, and you must decide what to do during that failure. This is the heart of CAP.

A partition means some nodes cannot talk to others (switch failure, cut cable, overloaded link, long GC pause that looks like a death). In a partition each side must choose: refuse requests (stay consistent) or answer with possibly stale data (stay available).

(The link between Node 1 and Node 2 is the one that breaks.)

Worked example. A bank balance replicated on two nodes. Link breaks. Client A withdraws 80 of 100 on Node 1; client B withdraws 80 on Node 2. If both succeed (available), the balance is -60 after merge. If Node 2 refuses (consistent), B sees an error but money is safe.

Industry examples. Network partitions are not rare: public post-mortems from major clouds and data stores report them regularly. Kyle Kingsbury's Jepsen tests have shown many databases losing data or breaking promised guarantees under partitions.

Everyday analogy. Two bank branches whose phone line is cut: they can either stop serving customers or serve them and reconcile later.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing partitions can be ignored on a LAN; they happen.
  • Treating CAP as a menu where you "pick two always".

notes.title: CAP theorem
notes.html:
CAP: in the presence of a network Partition, a system can provide either Consistency or Availability, not both.

  • Consistency (C), linearizability: every read sees the latest completed write, as if there were one copy.
  • Availability (A): every request to a non-failed node gets a (non-error) response, though not necessarily the newest data.
  • Partition tolerance (P): the system continues despite dropped messages between nodes.

Since partitions will happen, real choice is CP vs AP during a partition. When no partition exists, you can have both C and A.

CP examples:  ZooKeeper, etcd, HBase, Spanner (mostly), MongoDB (default majority writes),
              Redis cluster with strict settings (not guaranteed)
AP examples:  Cassandra (tunable), DynamoDB (eventually consistent reads default),
              Riak, CouchDB, DNS

(Classifications are simplifications; many systems are tunable per request.)

Worked example (quorum). 3 replicas, partition isolates 1. The side with 2 nodes holds a majority and keeps serving writes (CP); the isolated single node rejects writes. In an AP design, both sides accept writes and merge later via last-write-wins or vector clocks.

Decision gravity. CP vs AP is a business and data-model decision and effectively a one-way door: application code and invariants (for example "no oversell") assume the choice. Money, inventory counts, leader election: CP. Feeds, likes, carts, presence: AP, accepting repair logic.

Everyday analogy. Two ticket counters selling the last seat with a broken phone line: stop selling (consistent) or keep selling and risk double booking (available).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "CA system" for a distributed database; without P, you are a single node.
  • Using C in CAP as the same C as in ACID (they differ).
  • Saying MongoDB/Cassandra is "just AP/CP" without mentioning tunable settings.

notes.title: Beyond CAP: PACELC
notes.html:
PACELC: if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else (normal operation), choose Latency or Consistency. It captures the day-to-day trade-off CAP ignores: even with no partition, keeping replicas consistent costs latency.

System            If partition   Else (normal)   Label
DynamoDB (eventual) A             L               PA/EL
Cassandra (default) A             L               PA/EL
Cassandra QUORUM    A (partly)    C               tunable
MongoDB (default)   C             C               PC/EC (approx)
Spanner             C             C (pays latency) PC/EC
PNUTS (Yahoo)       C             L               PC/EL

(Labels are from the PACELC paper and later commentary; settings change them; confirm per version.)

Worked example. A write must reach 3 replicas in 3 regions (RTT 80 ms). Waiting for all: 80+ ms latency, strongly consistent. Waiting for 1: ~2 ms, replicas lag by tens of ms. That latency-vs-consistency choice happens on every write, partition or not.

Industry examples. Spanner uses TrueTime and waits out clock uncertainty (a few ms) at commit to get external consistency. DynamoDB offers per-read choice: eventual (cheaper, faster) or strongly consistent (costs 2x read capacity units and higher latency).

Decision gravity. Choosing sync vs async replication is mostly reversible via configuration but changes failure guarantees (RPO) and write latency, so review it per data class.

Everyday analogy. A group chat: waiting for everyone to confirm each message (slow, consistent) or posting right away (fast, some see it later).

Common interview traps.

  • Stopping at CAP when asked about trade-offs in normal operation.
  • Not quantifying latency cost of cross-region sync writes.

notes.title: Consistency models
notes.html:
A consistency model is the contract about what a reader may see. From strongest to weakest:

  • Linearizable (strong): operations appear to happen instantly at one point between call and return; real-time order respected. Reads always see the latest write. Cost: coordination (consensus, quorum, locks).
  • Sequential: all see the same order, not necessarily matching real time.
  • Causal: if A could have influenced B, everyone sees A before B; unrelated writes may appear in different orders.
  • Read-your-writes / session guarantees: you always see your own writes; monotonic reads (never go back in time); monotonic writes; writes-follow-reads.
  • Eventual: if writes stop, replicas converge. No promise on how soon or what you see meanwhile.

Worked example (read-your-writes). User updates profile name on primary; the next page read hits a replica lagging 300 ms and shows the old name. Fixes: read from primary for N seconds after a write, route by a version/LSN token the client carries, or sticky routing for that user. Facebook's early memcache/MySQL setup used "remote marker" tricks for the same issue.

Worked example (monotonic reads). User refreshes twice, hits replica A (up to date) then replica B (behind) and sees data disappear. Fix: pin a session to one replica or carry a minimum version.

Quorum arithmetic. With N replicas, write quorum W, read quorum R: if R + W > N, a read overlaps the latest write (N=3, W=2, R=2). Common configs: W=1,R=N (fast writes), W=N,R=1 (fast reads), W=R=quorum (balanced). Overlap alone does not give linearizability (sloppy quorums, clock-based last-write-wins and concurrent writes can still break it).

# Cassandra per-query consistency (CQL: CONSISTENCY LOCAL_QUORUM) with RF=3 per DC
# LOCAL_QUORUM = 2 of 3 replicas in the local data centre
# Reads + writes at LOCAL_QUORUM: R+W=4 > 3, overlap guaranteed within the DC

Industry examples. Spanner and etcd: linearizable. DynamoDB: eventual by default, strong optional. MongoDB: read concerns local, majority, linearizable and causal sessions. Amazon S3: strongly consistent for reads after writes since December 2020 (it was eventually consistent for overwrites before that).

Decision gravity. Choose per data type: balances and inventory need strong; timelines, counters and caches accept eventual. Weakening later breaks invariants the code assumed; strengthening later costs latency and often a migration.

Everyday analogy. News: a live scoreboard (strong) versus a newspaper tomorrow (eventual); in between, a friend who always repeats what you told them (read-your-writes).

Common interview traps.

  • Using "eventual consistency" to mean "wrong data"; it is a convergence guarantee.
  • Believing R + W > N gives linearizability.
  • Mixing up ACID consistency (constraints hold) with CAP consistency (linearizability).

notes.title: Resolving conflicts in AP systems
notes.html:
If both sides accept writes, you must merge later. Options:

  • Last write wins (LWW): keep the highest timestamp. Simple but loses data and depends on clocks (skew of tens of ms or more).
  • Vector clocks / version vectors: detect true concurrency, then keep siblings for the app to merge (Dynamo's shopping cart merged by union).
  • CRDTs: data types whose merges are commutative and convergent (counters, sets, registers); used in Redis Enterprise, Riak, collaborative editors.
  • Application-level merge or operational transforms for documents.
  • Read repair and anti-entropy (Merkle trees) bring replicas back together; hinted handoff stores writes for a down node.

Worked example. Cart on two nodes: one adds "book", the other adds "pen" during a partition. A set-union merge gives {book, pen}. With LWW, one item vanishes. For a "like" counter, a CRDT G-Counter (one slot per node, merge by max, value = sum) never loses increments.

Industry examples. Amazon Dynamo (vector clocks, cart merge), Cassandra (LWW per cell by default, with timestamps), Riak (siblings, CRDTs), Figma and Google Docs (CRDT or OT).

Decision gravity. Picking LWW is a hidden data-loss decision; choose it only when overwriting is acceptable (sensor reading), not for money.

Everyday analogy. Two people editing the same notes offline and merging later; either pick one version (lose edits) or combine both.

Common interview traps.

  • Using LWW with unsynchronised clocks and calling it safe.
  • Ignoring that clock skew can reorder writes even without a partition.

notes.title: Choosing in a design interview
notes.html:
Decide per feature, not per system. One product uses several consistency levels at once.

Feature                  Need                 Typical choice
Payment / balance        Linearizable         Single-leader SQL, Spanner, CP
Inventory (last unit)    Strong for decrement SQL row lock / conditional write
Order status             Read-your-writes     Primary reads after write
Profile page             Eventual + RYW       Replicas + sticky/version token
News feed, likes         Eventual             Cache, AP store, CRDT counter
Presence, typing         Best effort          In-memory, TTL
Leader election, locks   Linearizable         etcd / ZooKeeper (Raft / Zab)

Answer template: "For X, losing/duplicating means Y. So I need consistency level Z. I pay for it with latency L and lower availability under partition. For W the cost of staleness is small, so I use eventual and accept N ms of lag."

Worked example. E-commerce: product browsing and reviews are eventual from replicas and a cache (staleness up to 60 s is fine). Inventory reservation uses a conditional update UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = ? AND qty > 0 on the primary; payment uses idempotency keys and a single-leader database.

UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = 'S1' AND qty > 0;  -- 0 rows updated means out of stock

Industry examples. Amazon's retail catalogue is largely eventual while order placement is strict. Uber trip state needs strong consistency per trip (a trip must have exactly one driver) while driver location is best effort.

Decision gravity. The per-feature consistency table is the artefact worth stating in an interview; wrongly assigning "strong everywhere" makes the system slow and costly, "eventual everywhere" makes it incorrect.

Everyday analogy. A shop uses a precise till for money and a rough chalkboard for specials.

Common interview traps.

  • Declaring the whole system "CP" or "AP".
  • Not tying the choice to the business cost of a wrong read.
  • Forgetting to mention how you obtain read-your-writes in a replicated setup.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Partitions happen, so the real choice is C or A during a partition (CAP); with no partition, PACELC says latency vs consistency.
  • CAP "C" is linearizability, not ACID consistency; "A" means every live node answers.
  • Models from strong to weak: linearizable, sequential, causal, session guarantees (read-your-writes, monotonic reads), eventual.
  • Quorums: R + W > N overlaps the latest write but is not automatically linearizable.
  • AP systems need conflict resolution: LWW (lossy), vector clocks, CRDTs, app merges; use read repair and anti-entropy.
  • Choose consistency per feature by the business cost of a wrong read; money and locks strong, feeds and counters eventual.
